lede: Every appliance carries a power rating in watts, and every home has an energy meter counting units. This topic joins them: how fast an appliance transfers energy, how much it transfers in a given time, and what that energy costs.
can: Use E = P × t with the time in seconds, and P = I × V in either direction
Explain what a kilowatt-hour is and work out the units an appliance uses
Calculate the cost of using an appliance from its power rating and the price per unit

md: A kettle, a phone charger and a heater all say how many watts they use. That one number tells you how quickly each one transfers energy, and from it you can work out the energy used and the cost on the bill.

md: **Power** is the energy transferred each second, measured in **watts** (W). One watt is one joule every second, so a power rating says how fast an appliance turns electrical energy into heat, light or movement.

stem: The figure shows the energy a 1 600 W hairdryer transfers in its first four seconds. What does its power tell you, and how much energy does it transfer in 4 s? [2]

steps.working: Each second adds the same 1 600 J: that is what 1 600 W means.
steps.decision: Power is the energy transferred each second, so watts are joules per second.
Four equal blocks of 1 600 J.

steps.working: The 6 400 J is not a power: it is an amount of energy. Run the hairdryer longer and the joules grow, but the power stays 1 600 W.
steps.decision: The near-miss: power is a rate and energy an amount; only the energy grows with time.

prompt: A 40 W lamp is switched on. How much energy does it transfer each second, in joules?
explain: As in step 1 of the See it, power is the energy transferred each second, so 40 W means 40 joules every second, just as 1 600 W meant 1 600 J each second. The lamp transfers 40 J each second.

twin.prompt: A 9 W LED bulb is switched on. How much energy does it transfer each second, in joules?
twin.explain: Watts are joules per second, so a 9 W bulb transfers 9 J each second.

md: The energy is the rate multiplied by how long: **E = P × t**, with E in joules, P in watts and t in **seconds**. A time in minutes or hours is changed to seconds, on its own line, before you substitute.

title: The conversion that keeps costing marks
md: Summer 2025, both tiers: the equation was well recalled, but a significant number of candidates left the 10 minutes as 10 and lost marks. Summer 2024 saw the same slip. Convert to seconds first.

stem: The figure is for a 575 W dehumidifier that runs for 10 minutes. Calculate the energy it transfers. [4]

steps.decision: Write the equation first: it earns its own mark, and it fixes the units.
Minutes to seconds, on a line of its own, before you substitute.
Power in watts, time in seconds, and the unit: joules.

steps.working: Check on the graph: the line reaches 345 kJ at 600 s, and 345 000 J is 345 kJ.
steps.decision: The steady line is the steady power: each second adds the same energy.

prompt: A 150 W fan is left on for 8 minutes. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?
explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of the See it, change the time to seconds first: 8 × 60 = 480 s. Then E = P × t = 150 × 480 = 72 000 J. Multiplying by 8 would give a number 60 times too small.

twin.prompt: A 25 W radio is on for 40 minutes. How much energy does it transfer, in joules?
twin.explain: Seconds first: 40 × 60 = 2 400 s. Then E = P × t = 25 × 2 400 = 60 000 J.

text: 3. See it done: the four-mark energy question

md: The paper's usual shape is four marks: the equation, the time in seconds, the substitution and the answer with its unit. Each line earns its own mark, so write every one.

stem: A 1 800 W kettle is switched on for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy it transfers. [4]

steps.decision: The equation line, before any number.
The conversion, on its own line.
The substitution: watts and seconds.
The value with its unit.

title: Calculating energy transferred by appliances
why: Under four minutes on the energy an appliance transfers from its power and the time it runs, with a worked example and three to try. It is made for another board, which also uses equations CCEA does not ask for and never mentions the kilowatt-hour: for your paper, E = P × t and P = I × V are the two you need.

prompt: A 2 000 W heater runs for 2 minutes. Which calculation gives the energy it transfers, in joules?
explain: As in steps 2 and 3 of the See it, energy is power multiplied by time, and the time must be in seconds: 2 minutes is 120 s. So E = 2 000 × 120. Using 2 forgets the conversion, and dividing turns E = P × t into an equation that does not exist.

optionNotes.why: The minutes went in unconverted. E = P × t needs the time in seconds, so 2 minutes becomes 120 s first.
Dividing the power by the time is not an equation of this topic; energy is power multiplied by time.

twin.prompt: A 900 W microwave runs for 6 minutes. Which calculation gives the energy it transfers, in joules?
twin.explain: Energy is power × time with the time in seconds: 6 minutes is 360 s, so E = 900 × 360.

optionNotes.why: The 6 minutes must become 360 s before multiplying.
E = P × t multiplies; dividing makes an equation that does not exist.

caption: The ammeter gives the current, the voltmeter the voltage: multiply them for the power.

md: The current is the charge passing each second; the voltage is the energy each unit of charge carries. Multiply them and you get the energy transferred each second, which is the power: **P = I × V**, with P in watts, I in amps and V in volts.

title: Why multiplying works
md: Amps are coulombs per second and volts are joules per coulomb. Multiply them and the coulombs cancel, leaving joules per second: watts.

stem: In the figure the ammeter reads 3.2 A and the voltmeter reads 230 V. Calculate the power of the heater. [3]

steps.decision: The equation first.
Current in amps, voltage in volts.
Amps times volts gives watts.

prompt: A motor works on a 10 V supply and takes a current of 0.6 A. What is its power, in watts?
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of the See it, power is the current times the voltage: P = I × V = 0.6 × 10 = 6 W.

twin.prompt: A drill takes a current of 3.5 A from a 14 V battery. What is its power, in watts?
twin.explain: Current times voltage: P = I × V = 3.5 × 14 = 49 W.

md: A rating plate gives an appliance's voltage and power. For the current, rearrange P = I × V to **I = P ÷ V**. A power in kilowatts must first be changed to watts: multiply by 1000.

stem: The figure shows a toaster's rating plate: 230 V and 1.38 kW. Calculate the current it takes. [4]

steps.decision: Write the equation, then rearrange it for the current.
Kilowatts to watts before substituting.
Watts over volts.
The value with its unit.

prompt: An iron is rated 1.15 kW on the 230 V mains. What current does it take, in amps?
explain: As in steps 2 to 4 of the See it, change the power to watts, then divide by the voltage: 1.15 kW = 1 150 W, and I = P ÷ V = 1 150 ÷ 230 = 5 A. Dividing 1.15 by 230 would leave the kilowatts unconverted.

twin.prompt: A heater is rated 1.61 kW on the 230 V mains. What current does it take, in amps?
twin.explain: Watts first: 1.61 kW = 1 610 W. Then I = P ÷ V = 1 610 ÷ 230 = 7 A.

text: 6. The kilowatt-hour: energy on the bill

alt: The same energy measured two ways for a 2 kilowatt heater running 5 hours: 36 000 000 joules, or 10 kilowatt-hours.
caption: Two units for the same energy: joules for science, kilowatt-hours for the bill.

md: Joules are tiny for a home: a 2 kW heater uses millions in an evening. So electricity companies count energy in **kilowatt-hours** (kWh), also called **units**. One kilowatt-hour is the energy a 1 kW appliance uses in 1 hour, 1000 W × 3600 s = 3 600 000 J. It measures energy, not power.

stem: The figure is for a 2 kW heater running for 5 hours. How many kilowatt-hours does it use? [3]

steps.working: Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours
steps.decision: Kilowatt-hours need kilowatts and hours, not watts and seconds.
The power is already in kilowatts and the time in hours.
The value with its unit.

steps.working: In joules that is 36 000 000 J, as the figure shows: far too many to count on a bill.
steps.decision: The same energy in two units; the bill uses the larger one.

prompt: A 600 W heater is used for 5 hours. How many kilowatt-hours of energy does it use?
explain: As in steps 1 to 3 of the See it, multiply kilowatts by hours: first 600 W = 0.6 kW, then 0.6 × 5 = 3 kWh. Leaving the power in watts would give 3 000, a thousand times too many units.

twin.prompt: A 400 W freezer runs for 9 hours. How many kilowatt-hours of energy does it use?
twin.explain: Kilowatts times hours: 400 W = 0.4 kW, and 0.4 × 9 = 3.6 kWh.

alt: An energy meter on a brick wall: a glass dome over a white dial face marked kWh, with four small number dials in a row.
caption: A household energy meter counts kilowatt-hours: the kWh on its face is the unit the bill charges for.
prompt: This energy meter counts units. What is one unit, and how many would a 2 kW heater add in 5 hours?

md: The energy meter counts units. Units used = the later reading take away the earlier one: 52985 − 52718 = 267 units. Then **cost = units × price per unit**. Prices are in pence per unit; divide by 100 for pounds.

stem: A 1.5 kW heater is on for 4 hours, and electricity costs 32p per unit. Calculate the cost, in pounds. [4]

steps.decision: Kilowatts × hours gives the units.
Units × price per unit, in pence.
Pence to pounds: divide by 100.

prompt: An appliance uses 3 units of electricity. Each unit costs 40p. What is the cost, in pence?
explain: As in step 2 of the See it, cost is units times the price of one unit: 3 × 40 = 120p, which is £1.20.

twin.prompt: A tumble dryer uses 7 units, and each unit costs 35p. What is the cost, in pence?
twin.explain: Units times the price per unit: 7 × 35 = 245p, which is £2.45.

md: **A plate with a value missing** (Summer 2021 and Summer 2024). Two of power, current and voltage are given: write the equation that joins them before any number. In 2024, starting from power = energy ÷ time scored nothing.
**A cost built from the units.** Summer 2021 and Summer 2024 set a [5] cost question. Change watts to kilowatts and minutes to hours, find the units, then multiply by the price.
**Tick the box.** Summer 2021 and Summer 2024: a unit of electricity is a kilowatt-hour, which measures energy: a 1000 W appliance used for 3600 seconds.

stem: A phone charger's plate shows its power, 6 W, and its current, 0.5 A, but the voltage has worn off. Calculate the voltage. [3]

steps.working: The plate gives power and current, so use the power equation rearranged for voltage: $V = P \div I$
steps.decision: Start from the equation that joins the two values the plate gives.
Watts over amps.
The value with its unit.

prompt: The rating plate shown gives the voltage and the current, but the power has been left blank. What should the first line of your working be?
explain: As in step 1 of the See it, start from the equation joining the two values the plate gives: current and voltage give power through P = I × V, so 5.0 × 230 = 1 150 W. The plate gives no energy or time, and V = I × R is about resistance.

optionNotes.why: Power is energy over time, but the plate gives neither; in Summer 2024 a working that started from it scored nothing.
That links voltage, current and resistance; the plate asks for power, which needs P = I × V.

twin.prompt: A plate gives a heater's power and its voltage, but not its current. What should the first line of your working be?
twin.explain: The power equation joins power, current and voltage; rearranged for the current it is I = P ÷ V.

optionNotes.why: That rearrangement is upside down: dividing the voltage by the power does not give the current.
Multiplying power by voltage gives no current; divide the power by the voltage.

md:
Say what power is: the energy transferred each second, in watts.
Use E = P × t with the time in seconds, converting minutes first.
Use P = I × V, and I = P ÷ V with kilowatts changed to watts.
Find units as kW × hours, and cost as units × price per unit.

Expect [3] for P = I × V or E = P × t (equation, substitution, answer), a fourth mark when a time must be converted, and [5] for a cost worked through the units. Write the equation first, convert units on their own line, and give the unit: J, W, A, kWh, p. Stuck? Ask which two quantities you have and which equation joins them.
